title: Hanukkah: Maoz Tzur
hookLine: a medieval song sung after lighting, recalling many rescues

cards: The candles are lit. The blessings are said. Kids are already eyeing the doughnuts.
Then, in many homes, before anyone moves, someone starts a song. Plenty of people know the tune but not most of the words; they hum through the middle and come back loud for the end.
Many families sing only the first verse. But it has six, and if you read them all, it isn't only a song about Hanukkah. It's a song about a lot of nights like this one.

teach.b: The song is called Maoz Tzur. Maoz means stronghold, a fortress. Tzur means rock.
The Torah uses rock as a name for God; in the old Jewish translation, Moses sings, "The Rock, His work is perfect." So the song opens by calling God the fortress-rock of my salvation. Who wrote it?
The poet signed it the way medieval Hebrew poets liked: the first letters of the first five verses spell a name, Mordechai. Nobody knows for certain who this Mordechai was. Now the verses.
The first looks forward to a rebuilt Temple.

The second remembers slavery in Egypt, and the way out. The third, the exile to Babylon, and the return after seventy years. The fourth, Haman, who wanted to destroy the Jews of Persia, in the story Purim tells.
Only the fifth gets to the Greeks, the Hasmoneans and the jar of oil. And the sixth, likely added later, asks for one more rescue, in the poet's own time.
So Hanukkah, in this song, is one link in a chain. Danger, then rescue. Danger, then rescue.
People sang it in places where the danger was not ancient history.
The English version some families sing, Rock of Ages, is a loose adaptation rather than a translation. And Sephardi and Mizrahi families often sing other songs, or other tunes.
The words that travel everywhere are the first two: fortress, rock.

how: In many Ashkenazi homes, the family sings Maoz Tzur together after lighting the Hanukkah candles each night, usually the first verse; Sephardi and Mizrahi families often sing other hymns or Psalm 30.

games.q: you're a medieval Hebrew poet who wants to sign your Hanukkah song, but signatures aren't done. what do you do?
o: put your name in the last line.
spell your name with the first letters of the verses.
games.why: the first letters of the first five verses spell Mordechai. the signature hides in plain sight.

practice: Hear a song that has carried you through something, a hard year, a long drive, a loss; it doesn't have to be religious. Hum its first line quietly, or just in your head.
Let it sit beside one time in your own story when you got through.
